newsitem.title: USA: Kantor "making plans" to leave Commerce Department.
newsitem.headline: Kantor "making plans" to leave Commerce Department.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of Commerce Mickey Kantor indicated on Wednesday he was planning to resign and return to private life, a spokesman for his department said.
"He is making plans to return to private life," the spokesman said when asked whether Kantor planned to step down.
No further details were given, and the timing of his possible departure was uncertain.
President Bill Clinton, on board Air Force One, acknowledged he had spoken to Kantor.
"I have talked to Mickey Kantor but we haven't reached a final decision," Clinton told reporters as he headed back to Washington from Little Rock, Arkansas, where he celebrated his election victory.

Kantor served as U.S. trade representative before Clinton asked him to replace the late Ron Brown as secretary of commerce. Brown died earlier this year in a plane crash while taking a group of corporate executives on a trade mission to Bosnia and Croatia.
The Commerce Department became a target for elimination last year by congressional Republicans anxious to cut the size of government and reduce federal spending.

The agency survived the budget battle, but many political analysts and department employees believe it will be targeted again this year, particularly in light of recent campaign fund-raising scandals involving John Huang. Huang was formerly a high-ranking official in the Commerce Department's International Trade Administration.

There had been widespread speculation in Washington that Kantor, said to be unhappy as commerce chief, would move to another position during Clinton's second term, possibly that of White House chief of staff or attorney general.

A close friend of Clinton, Kantor worked on the president's successful 1992 campaign and led the Clinton campaign's negotiations with the campaign of Republican challenger Bob Dole on this year's presidential debates.

As U.S. trade representative, Kantor negotiated a number of key trade agreements. He completed negotiations for the United States in the global talks that created the new World Trade Organisation and the North America Free Trade Agreement, which united Canada, the United States and Mexico in a trade zone. He also negotiated a 1995 deal with Tokyo to open Japan's car and car parts markets to more U.S.-made products.

Before joining the Clinton administration, Kantor was an attorney in Los Angeles and was well known in California political circles. In 1976 he was chairman of Jerry Brown's presidential campaign, and in 1984 he led Walter Mondale's efforts in California.
